SEND Life Transition: Free Wellbeing Support for the Move to College

Why I created SEND Life Transition, a free YouTube channel supporting the emotional wellbeing of young people with SEND as they move from school to college, and what it offers families and educators.

By Gibson Nyendwa · 29 October 2026 · 5 min read

SEND & Inclusive Education: Special Educational Needs and Disabilities.

Moving from school to college is a big change for any young person. For young people with SEND (special educational needs and disabilities), it can be one of the hardest moments in their education: new buildings, new people, new routines and far more independence, often all at once.

In a short video for the SEND Life Transition channel, I explain why I set up the channel and how it is meant to help. This article walks through the same ideas in more detail, adds some context for families and staff in England, and suggests a few practical first steps. Where I add information that is not in the video, I say so and link to the source.

Why the move to college matters so much

In the video I describe the transition to college as a critical point of vulnerability for young people with SEND. Three things tend to come together.

  • Routines change. The timetable, the journey, the building and the faces are all new, and the structure that school provided is often looser.
  • Executive functioning demands rise. Executive functioning means the mental skills we use to plan, organise, start tasks, manage time and keep track of what we are doing. College usually asks young people to do much more of this for themselves.
  • Emotional support can be harder to reach. The video points out that mental health resources are often not accessible enough for the young people who need them most.

When these pressures stack up, some young people find it difficult to settle or to stay on their course. That is the gap SEND Life Transition is trying to help with.

Additional context for England: an education, health and care (EHC) plan can support children and young people aged up to 25 who need more help than is available through ordinary SEN support, and young people aged 16 to 25 can ask their local authority for an EHC needs assessment themselves (GOV.UK). Wales, Scotland and Northern Ireland have their own systems, so check the guidance where you live.

What SEND Life Transition is

SEND Life Transition is a free YouTube channel. Because it is online and free, young people, families and staff can use it whenever they need it, at their own pace, and come back to a video as often as they like.

The video describes the channel as peer-based psychological support delivered through accessible video, with a supportive tone. In practice, that means short, plain-English videos that talk with young people rather than at them, about the things that worry them most: starting college, managing feelings, friendships, independence and knowing their rights.

It is educational content, not a clinical service. If a young person is struggling, their college's student support team, their GP or the people who already know them well remain the right places to turn.

The ideas behind the content

In the video, I explain that the content draws on what we know about stress and self-compassion. In everyday terms, it covers three things.

  • How stress shows up in the brain and body. The video refers to the amygdala, a part of the brain involved in noticing threats, and the prefrontal cortex, which helps with planning, decision-making and self-control. When we feel overwhelmed, it can be much harder to think things through calmly.
  • Practical ways to calm the body's stress response, so that thinking and planning become easier again.
  • Self-compassion: treating yourself with the same understanding you would show a friend, rather than criticising yourself for finding things hard.

The video also mentions mirror neuron theory as part of its approach to emotional regulation. It is worth knowing that this is a theory researchers still discuss and debate, so I treat it as one way of thinking about how we learn from each other, not as settled fact.

For example (an illustration, not a real case): a student who freezes at the start of a new class might learn, through a short video, to notice that their body is in a stress response, take a few slow breaths, and remind themselves that feeling nervous on a first day is normal. Small steps like these are what the channel is built around.

Who the channel is for

  • Young people with SEND who are preparing for college or already there.
  • Parents and carers supporting a young person through the change.
  • Teaching Assistants and tutors working alongside students day to day.
  • SENCOs (Special Educational Needs Coordinators) and other professionals planning transitions.

How it connects to the Global Goals

The video links the project to three of the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals: Goal 3, Good Health and Well-being; Goal 4, Quality Education; and Goal 10, Reduced Inequalities. The aim is to remove barriers to good-quality emotional support, so that it is not only available to those who can pay for it or reach it easily.

What comes next

The video sets out a plan in four phases. These are plans, not services that are running today.

  • Phases 1 and 2: grow the online community, make videos on topics that viewers ask for, and develop structured digital courses, including a transition toolkit.
  • Phases 3 and 4: bring the online and offline worlds together through in-person workshops and training for educators.
  • Finally, evaluate how well the approach works and share the findings through academic publication.

Why this project matters to me

SEND Life Transition grew out of my studies with Atlantic International University, where I have been learning about emotion, personality and social cognition. As I say in the video, it is my way of turning academic theory into something practical that young people, families and educators can use.

Practical first steps

  • Young people: pick one topic that worries you about college and watch a single short video on it. You do not have to watch everything at once.
  • Parents and carers: watch a video together and use it to start a conversation about what feels hard and what might help.
  • Teaching Assistants, tutors and SENCOs: use a short video as a starting point for transition conversations, then link it to the support your setting already offers.
  • Everyone: tell the channel what you would like covered next. Requested topics are part of the plan for the next phase.
